opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core issue is that upsampling, in the classical sense, is fundamentally an interpolation problem. You take the pixels you have and estimate the ones in between: bilinear, bicubic, even many learned upsamplers are essentially trying to fill in a denser grid in a smooth, plausible way. That works reasonably well when the low-resolution image is a faithful, downsampled version of some real high-resolution scene, because the information you need is at least partially encoded there.

AI-generated images break that assumption. When a diffusion model or another generative model produces an image at, say, 512 by 512, there is no "true" high-resolution original behind it. The fine detail was never there to begin with. So if you just upsample, you magnify whatever the model produced, including its artifacts: slightly incoherent textures, smeared high-frequency regions, odd edges, hair that turns into mush, text that's almost but not quite legible. You get a bigger image, but not a better one. Often it looks worse, because those flaws become more visible at higher resolution.

What you actually need is something closer to generation than interpolation. You have to synthesize new high-frequency content that is consistent with the semantics and structure of the low-resolution image: real texture for fabric, believable pores on skin, crisp geometry on buildings. That means the super-resolution model needs a strong prior about what the world looks like at fine scales, and it has to make decisions, not just average neighboring pixels.

There's also a consistency dimension. Generative images tend to have local inconsistencies, so a good super-resolution approach should correct or refine content, not just faithfully preserve it. Unlike classical super-resolution, fidelity to the input isn't the only goal. You're balancing staying true to the composition and intent of the generated image against fixing the things the base model got wrong.

And practically, there's efficiency. Running the full generative model at high resolution is expensive and often produces repetition or structural problems because the models weren't trained at that scale. So the sweet spot is to generate at a manageable resolution, then use a dedicated model that adds detail intelligently, guided by the content, ideally in a few steps rather than a long diffusion process. That's why we think of it less as upsampling and more as conditional detail generation.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that upsampling only interpolates existing pixels and cannot supply the missing fine detail, then says super-resolution must generate new detail consistent with the image’s semantics and structure.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention adding noise in latent space or retaining access to the image’s original generation prompt.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the thing people often miss is that a generated image, say from a diffusion model, isn't a downsampled version of some pristine high-resolution ground truth that's sitting out there waiting to be recovered. That's the implicit assumption behind classical super-resolution. You take a low-res input, you assume there was a high-frequency signal that got lost through a known degradation, and you try to hallucinate it back in a way that's consistent with the input.

But with a generated image, the "low-res" version is the only version that ever existed. The model produced it at, say, 512 or 1024, and whatever structure is there is what the generator decided to put there at that scale. So if you just upsample, even with a very good learned upsampler, you're essentially smoothing and sharpening the existing content. You get bigger pixels, maybe cleaner edges, but you don't get new semantic detail. The texture on a fabric, the individual strands of hair, the lettering on a sign in the background, those were never resolved by the generator, so there's nothing to recover. You end up with something that looks high-resolution at a glance but has a kind of plasticky, oversmoothed quality when you actually zoom in.

The second problem is that generative artifacts get upsampled too. If the base model produced a slightly malformed hand or inconsistent geometry, upsampling faithfully preserves that, and now it's just a larger malformed hand. A pure upsampler is trained to be faithful to its input, so by design it won't correct anything.

So in our view, super-resolving generated content really has to be a generative problem itself. You need a model that understands the semantics of what's in the image and can synthesize plausible high-frequency detail that's consistent with the global structure, while also having some latitude to fix local inconsistencies. That means conditioning on the low-res image but not being enslaved to it, and ideally having access to the same prompt or the same latent context the original generator used so the added detail is coherent with the intent rather than generic. Upsampling is one component in that pipeline, but on its own it's just resizing with better interpolation.

r001.rationale: It explains that upsampling cannot create semantic details the generator never resolved, such as hair strands or fabric texture.

r002.rationale: It mentions access to the original prompt or latent context, but does not link that to adding noise in each latent space.

astra-6.text:
Upsampling increases the number of pixels, but it doesn’t necessarily increase the amount of meaningful detail. If you simply interpolate an image, you’re estimating values between existing pixels. You can make the image larger, but the textures and fine structures that were missing are still missing.

For AI-generated images, there’s also the question of whether the content is coherent. If the original image has a distorted structure, upsampling will preserve that distortion. So super-resolution needs to do more than resize: it needs to generate plausible detail while respecting the image’s content and structure. The challenge is adding that detail without changing what the image is supposed to represent.

r001.rationale: It says interpolation enlarges the image without restoring missing meaningful detail, so super-resolution must generate plausible detail.

r002.rationale: It does not mention adding noise in latent spaces or retaining access to the original generation prompt.

sol-6.1.text: Upsampling gives you more pixels, but it doesn’t necessarily give you more information. If a generated image has missing texture or an inconsistent structure, simply enlarging it preserves those problems—it may just make them more visible. For super-resolution, we need to infer plausible fine detail while keeping it consistent with the image’s content. So the challenge is not just increasing resolution; it’s improving detail without changing what the image represents.

r001.rationale: It says upsampling adds pixels without information and that super-resolution must infer fine detail consistent with the image’s content, identifying the lack of meaningful detail as the limitation.

r002.rationale: It does not mention adding noise in latent spaces or retaining access to the original generation prompt.
